## Limitations of the evaluation

The paper acknowledges limits that are important to keep in mind:
------

Together these pieces build an empirical case that DPO is competitive with PPO on preference learning tasks while being simpler to train and less...–Luce) depend only on reward differences, the partition function disappears and we can express the probability that humans prefer y1 over y2 purely in terms of pi and pi_ref. This leads directly to a simple cross-entropy objective over policies:
------
\title{Blogs about the Paper: "Direct Preference Optimization: Your Language Model is Secretly a Reward Model"}

max_pi E_{x,y~pi}[ r(x,y) ] - beta * KL[ pi || pi_ref ],

then the... that removes the need for an explicit reward learner and an RL training loop. That simplicity translates directly into practical gains: fewer moving parts, lower compute, and easier reproducibility — exactly the properties that make preference learning accessible to more ML teams.<|endoftext|>

### How exactly does the partition function cancel out in the DPO derivation?
Question:

## Limitations of the evaluation

The paper acknowledges limits that are important to keep in mind:
------
\title{Blogs about the Paper: "Direct Preference Optimization: Your Language Model is Secretly a Reward Model"}

Together these pieces build an empirical case that DPO is competitive with PPO on preference learning tasks while being simpler to train and less...–Luce) depend only on reward differences, the partition function disappears and we can express the probability that humans prefer y1 over y2 purely in terms of pi and pi_ref. This leads directly to a simple cross-entropy objective over policies:
------
\title{Blogs about the Paper: "Direct Preference Optimization: Your Language Model is Secretly a Reward Model"}

max_pi E_{x,y~pi}[ r(x,y) ] - beta * KL[ pi || pi_ref ],

then the... that removes the need for an explicit reward learner and an RL training loop. That simplicity translates directly into practical gains: fewer moving parts, lower compute, and easier reproducibility — exactly the properties that make preference learning accessible to more ML teams.<|endoftext|>

If you expect systematic length differences in your pairs, you should consider pairing by length or using a per-token normalization deliberately, while understanding that this changes the objective the model is optimizing.

## Limitations of the evaluation

The paper acknowledges limits that are important to keep in mind:
------
\title{Blogs about the Paper: "Direct Preference Optimization: Your Language Model is Secretly a Reward Model"}

Together these pieces build an empirical case that DPO is competitive with PPO on preference learning tasks while being simpler to train and less...–Luce) depend only on reward differences, the partition function disappears and we can express the probability that humans prefer y1 over y2 purely in terms of pi and pi_ref. This leads directly to a simple cross-entropy objective over policies:
------
\title{Blogs about the Paper: "Direct Preference Optimization: Your Language Model is Secretly a Reward Model"}

max_pi E_{x,y~pi}[ r(x,y) ] - beta * KL[ pi || pi_ref ],

then the... that removes the need for an explicit reward learner and an RL training loop. That simplicity translates directly into practical gains: fewer moving parts, lower compute, and easier reproducibility — exactly the properties that make preference learning accessible to more ML teams.<|endoftext|>

If you expect systematic length differences in your pairs, you should consider pairing by length or using a per-token normalization deliberately, while understanding that this changes the objective the model is optimizing.

## Limitations of the evaluation

The paper acknowledges limits that are important to keep in mind:

This leads directly to a simple cross-entropy objective over policies:
------
\title{Blogs about the Paper: "Direct Preference Optimization: Your Language Model is Secretly a Reward Model"}

max_pi E_{x,y~pi}[ r(x,y) ] - beta * KL[ pi || pi_ref ],

then the... that removes the need for an explicit reward learner and an RL training loop. That simplicity translates directly into practical gains: fewer moving parts, lower compute, and easier reproducibility — exactly the properties that make preference learning accessible to more ML teams.<|endoftext|>

### How exactly does the partition function cancel out in the DPO derivation?
